turns.replyText:
Can you explain the main options in simple terms?

Totally get it, there ARE a lot of choices. Here are the main rose options in simple, beginner-friendly buckets:

By shape/how they grow
Shrub/bush roses: Round, bushy plants. Great for beds, along walkways, or near patios. Easiest place to start.
Climbing roses: Long canes that need support (fence, arch, trellis). Beautiful but need more tying/training.
Groundcover/landscape roses: Low, spreading plants that cover an area. Good for slopes or borders.
By flower style & use
Hybrid tea roses: Classic “long-stem” roses, usually one big bloom per stem. Great for cutting and vases.
Floribunda roses: Lots of medium-sized blooms in clusters. Very colorful, great for showy beds.
English / “old-fashioned” style roses: Full, many-petaled, often very fragrant blooms. Romantic, cottage-garden look.
By blooming habit
Repeat/continuous bloomers: Flower, rest, flower again through the season. Most people prefer these.
Once-blooming roses: One big flush of flowers per year, often in spring, then mostly foliage.
By fragrance
Strong fragrance: Big perfume, great near doors, paths, and patios.
Light/no fragrance: Still beautiful, sometimes better if you’re sensitive to scents.
By your garden conditions
Full sun: At least 6 hours of direct sun daily (roses love this).
Partial shade: About 4+ hours of sun; some varieties handle this better than others.
Hardiness zone: This is your climate rating. On our site you can set your zone at the top so you only see roses that can thrive where you live.

Newer gardeners say some very similar things again and again in their reviews. A few common themes:

It settles in and blooms quickly
People often mention getting leaves and buds within a few weeks of planting. For example, one reviewer of an English shrub rose said it bloomed about 4 weeks after planting and called it “very beautiful” even though their area is tough for roses.
Another beginner growing a floribunda in a pot mentioned it “fully leafed out” within about a month and was already expecting buds soon.
It feels easier than expected
New growers talk about planting, watering, and then being pleasantly surprised that the rose “took off” without a lot of complicated care.
Some mention that while other roses in their garden are struggling, their Heirloom rose is establishing well, which makes them feel more confident as beginners.
They’re happy with the quality and support
Reviews often mention being “very happy with Heirloom” and planning to buy more once they see how their first rose performs.

Is there anything else a beginner needs to get started?

You’re asking all the right questions. To keep it simple, here’s what most beginners “actually” need beyond the rose itself:

Good planting spot
Sun: Aim for full sun (about 6+ hours of direct sun).
Soil: Drains well (no spots that stay soggy after rain).
Basic tools
A hand trowel or small shovel for planting.
Gloves (roses have thorns, even “thornless” types can have a few).
A watering can or hose with a gentle setting.
Helpful amendments (optional but very nice to have) If you want to give your first rose a strong start, these are beginner-friendly:

Get Growing Bundle
A simple “all-in-one” set of our favorite amendments, so you do not have to overthink it.

Mint compost
Mixed into the planting hole or used on top of the soil, it helps retain moisture and protects roots.

Founders Fish Fertilizer
A gentle fertilizer you can use about every 4 weeks during the growing season to support healthy growth, especially in the first year.
